items.prompt: In the acronym POUR, what does the P stand for?
choices: Perceivable
Predictable
Programmable
items.explanation: POUR is Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.

items.prompt: A video has no captions. Which principle does that mainly break?
choices: Operable: the player cannot be driven
Robust: the player breaks on old tech
Perceivable: the audio is not sensed
items.explanation: Deaf and hard-of-hearing users cannot sense the audio, so the content is not perceivable.

items.prompt: A menu opens only when the mouse hovers over it. Which principle fails?
choices: Perceivable
Operable
Understandable
items.explanation: Without a keyboard equivalent, anyone not using a mouse cannot operate it.

items.prompt: An error says only "Invalid input". Which principle fails?
choices: Understandable: it names no fix
Perceivable: it cannot be seen
Robust: it breaks on old browsers
items.explanation: The message can be seen but does not say what to fix, so it is not understandable.

items.prompt: A checkbox is a styled div that screen readers do not recognize. Which principle fails?
choices: Operable
Perceivable
Robust
items.explanation: Robust means working across browsers and assistive technology; an unrecognized widget does not.

items.prompt: How many principles make up POUR?
choices: Three
Four
Five
items.explanation: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust: four.

items.prompt: Can a single page fail more than one principle at once?
choices: Yes, from unrelated causes
No, only one at a time at most
Only when viewed on mobile screens
items.explanation: The checkout failed Perceivable and Understandable together, from two separate root causes.

items.prompt: Which plain question belongs to Operable?
choices: Can it be sensed at all?
Is it predictable and clear to read?
Can it be used without a mouse?
items.explanation: Operable asks whether people can drive the interface with different input methods.

items.prompt: A date picker works with mouse and keyboard, but a voice-control tool cannot find or name any of its buttons. Which principle fails?
choices: Robust: it exposes no roles or names that assistive tech needs
Perceivable: the dates are too small for anyone to read
Operable: the keyboard handlers are missing from the picker
Understandable: the picker uses an unfamiliar date format for its month labels
items.explanation: Voice control reads the accessibility tree. If roles and names are missing, the failure is about working with assistive tech, which is Robust.
items.reference:
POUR at a glance
👁️ Perceivable: can it be sensed at all?
🖱️ Operable: can it be used without a mouse?
💡 Understandable: is it predictable and clear?
🔧 Robust: does it work across assistive tech?
Why: every barrier breaks at least one of these four, and one defect can break two at once.
items.learnMore:
Four preconditions, not four features

Each principle is a precondition for the next: if a control cannot be sensed, its operability and clarity never get a chance. That is why one failed principle can block a whole task.

Common mistake

Counting a page as fine because three of the four hold. Each principle can stand alone as a complete blocker.
items.reflection: Pick a door, an appliance, or a form you used today. Which of the four questions would it fail first for someone with a different set of abilities than yours?

items.prompt: A form has an icon-only submit button with no text alternative and an error that says "Something went wrong". Which pair of principles fails?
choices: Operable and Robust together
Perceivable and Understandable
Perceivable and Operable together
Robust and Understandable together
items.explanation: A missing text alternative is a Perceivable failure; an unhelpful error is an Understandable failure.

The captions fix one principle, but the unreachable button still fails Operable
The unreachable button is a captioning problem to solve
items.explanation: Fixing one principle does not cover another. Captions are Perceivable; reaching Play by keyboard is Operable.

The fourth principle counts double in a conformance test result

items.prompt: Which group benefits most from captions?
choices: Blind and low-vision users
Deaf and hard-of-hearing users
Users with limited fine motor control
items.explanation: Captions turn audio into text.

items.prompt: Text alternatives on images mainly help which group?
choices: Blind users with screen readers
Deaf users who rely on captions
Users who cannot use a mouse at all
items.explanation: A screen reader reads the alternative text aloud.

items.prompt: Full keyboard operation mainly helps which group?
choices: Users with color blindness
Deaf users who need captions
Users who cannot use a mouse
items.explanation: Keyboard access works without precise pointing.

items.prompt: Which design choice helps users with memory or attention differences?
choices: Smaller text with tighter spacing
Clear errors that say what to fix
Hiding hints once typing starts
items.explanation: Clear, forgiving feedback reduces what a person must remember.

items.prompt: Meaning carried by color alone is a problem for which users?
choices: Users with color blindness
Users who rely on captions
Users with limited hearing
items.explanation: If color is the only signal, people who cannot tell the colors apart miss it.

items.prompt: Glare on a phone screen in sunlight is an example of a...
choices: Permanent hearing loss
Browser compatibility bug
Situational limitation
items.explanation: Anyone can face a temporary limit that resembles a disability.

items.prompt: Why does accessible design often help everyone?
choices: It makes pages smaller to download everywhere
Many everyday limits resemble disabilities
It removes the need for any later testing
items.explanation: A sprained wrist or a noisy room creates the same needs.

items.prompt: Which feature helps someone with a hand tremor?
choices: Large, well-spaced tap targets
Timed prompts that expire fast
Hover-only menus with no keys
items.explanation: Bigger targets tolerate imprecise pointing.

items.prompt: A signup form shows "Email" only as placeholder text, which vanishes once typing starts. Which need is hit hardest?
choices: Auditory: the field makes no sound when it is focused
Cognitive: the hint vanishes just when memory needs it
Motor: the field is too small for a fingertip to tap
Visual: the placeholder is always invisible to everyone
items.explanation: Anyone who looks away mid-form loses the field's identity; this hurts memory and attention differences most.
items.reference:
Needs map
👁️ Visual → text alternatives, contrast, not color alone
👂 Auditory → captions, transcripts, visual alerts
✋ Motor → keyboard use, large targets, no tight timers
🧠 Cognitive → clear language, steady layout, helpful errors
Why: different abilities need different fixes, so one accommodation never covers everyone.
items.learnMore:
One redesign, several unmet needs

The checkout hit Visual (faint error), Cognitive (vanishing hint) and more at once. Mapping a defect to categories shows who it blocks and which fix serves them.

Common mistake

Picturing only a fully blind screen-reader user and treating the rest as edge cases.
items.reflection: Think of a time you used a device with one hand, in bright sun, or in a loud room. Which category's fix would have helped you right then?

items.prompt: An app signals new messages only with a beep. Adding a visual badge helps which people?
choices: Only users who were born deaf and use sign language
Only users who have a screen reader running
Deaf users and anyone in a noisy or muted setting
Only users whose devices are set to silent mode
items.explanation: The same fix serves permanent, temporary, and situational limits.

items.prompt: Which conformance level is the usual legal and industry target?
choices: A
AAA
AA
items.explanation: AA is what most laws and procurement standards reference.

items.prompt: What is the minimum contrast for normal body text at AA?
items.explanation: AA requires at least 4.5:1 for normal text.

items.prompt: What contrast does AAA ask for in normal body text?
items.explanation: AAA raises the bar to 7:1.

items.prompt: Which is an example of a Level A requirement?
choices: Captions for live audio streams
Contrast of at least 7:1 for text
Every image has alternative text
items.explanation: Alt text is a basic barrier removal criterion.

items.prompt: Which level is the strictest?
choices: AA (4.5:1 text)
AAA (7:1 text)
A (no text ratio)
items.explanation: The levels are ordered A, AA, AAA by strictness.

items.prompt: Is AAA usually required for a whole site?
choices: No, it is rarely required site-wide
Yes, every public site must meet it
Only for sites that include video
items.explanation: Some AAA criteria are very hard to meet for all content.

items.prompt: What does a conformance level give a team?
choices: A guarantee of zero bugs
A replacement for user testing
A checkable target
items.explanation: Criteria can be tested one by one.

items.prompt: Large text needs what minimum contrast at AA?
items.explanation: Large text is easier to read, so AA relaxes it to 3:1.

items.prompt: A vendor writes "our product is WCAG compliant." What is the best follow-up question?
choices: Which framework is the product built with, and by whom?
How many users has the product reached to date?
Which level and version, and how was it tested?
Which team wrote the vendor's marketing page copy?
items.explanation: A claim needs a level, a version, and a method before it can be checked.
items.reference:
WCAG levels
🅰️ A: remove total blockers (alt text)
✅ AA: the usual target (text 4.5:1)
🏆 AAA: strictest (text 7:1), used selectively
📏 large text at AA only needs 3:1
Why: a level turns "accessible" into a claim you can test criterion by criterion.
items.learnMore:
A claim is only as good as its scope

"WCAG compliant" says little until it names a level, a version, and how it was tested. AA is the common legal and procurement bar; AAA is applied to specific content because it can rule out whole palettes.

Common mistake

Hearing "accessible" as a yes/no label instead of asking which level was met.
items.reflection: Think of a standard in another field, such as food safety or building codes. What would you ask a vendor to see before believing they meet it?

items.prompt: Body text measures 5.2:1 on its background. What is the verdict?
choices: Fails AA, passes AAA
Passes both AA and AAA
Fails both AA and AAA
Passes AA, fails AAA
items.explanation: 5.2 is at least 4.5 but below 7.

items.prompt: What does a screen reader actually read?
choices: The accessibility tree
The page's CSS
A screenshot of the page
items.explanation: The browser builds a tree of roles, names, and states for assistive tech.

items.prompt: Which three properties does the tree compute for a control?
choices: Color, size, and position
Font, margin, and weight
Role, name, and state
items.explanation: Role says what it is, name what to call it, state its current condition.

items.prompt: Is CSS visual styling read by assistive technology?
choices: Yes, always
No
Only for buttons
items.explanation: Styling is not part of the accessibility tree.

items.prompt: What role does a native button element get?
choices: Button
Generic
Link
items.explanation: The HTML spec gives it that role automatically.

items.prompt: What role does a div with only an onclick get?
choices: Link, since it responds to clicks
Button, since it can be clicked
Generic, effectively nothing
items.explanation: It does not exist in the tree as an interactive control.

items.prompt: Which of these is a state?
choices: A name such as Close or Save
Expanded or collapsed
A link or a heading
items.explanation: State describes a condition that can change, such as expanded.

items.prompt: What question does the accessible name answer?
choices: What do I call this?
What color is this?
Where is this on screen?
items.explanation: The name is the label a person would use to refer to the control.

items.prompt: Which of these reads the tree?
choices: A print stylesheet
An image compression tool
Voice control software
items.explanation: Screen readers, switch devices, and voice control all use it.

items.prompt: A button has aria-label="Close" and visible text "Dismiss". What does a screen reader announce as its name?
choices: Dismiss, because visible text always takes priority over labels
Close Dismiss, because both names are joined in order
Nothing, because two competing names cancel each other out
Close, because aria-label outranks the element's own text
items.explanation: In the lookup order aria-label comes before the element's own text content.
items.reference:
From markup to speech
🧱 HTML / DOM
➡️ browser builds the accessibility tree
🏷️ per element: role + name + state
🔊 screen reader, switch, voice control read the tree
Why: assistive tech reads this tree, not the pixels and not the CSS.
items.learnMore:
Role, name, state

A native button gets its role for free. The name comes from a fixed lookup: aria-labelledby, then aria-label, then label or own text, then title. The state (checked, expanded) must be kept current.

Common mistake

Assuming that what looks like a button on screen is a button in the tree.
items.reflection: Pick an object whose looks mislead about its function, like a painted-on door. What would its "role, name, and state" be to someone who cannot see it?

items.prompt: A button holds only an SVG icon with no text, label, or aria-label. What does a screen reader announce?
choices: Just "button", since the name is empty
"Icon", read from the SVG file name
"Close", guessed from the icon's shape
Nothing at all, because the button is hidden
items.explanation: The lookup runs out of sources, so the role is exposed with no name.

It stays announced as not checked
It is announced as a link instead of a checkbox
It is skipped entirely when tabbing through
items.explanation: The tree's state only changes when markup or script updates it; color is invisible to it.

items.prompt: A dialog has aria-labelledby pointing at a heading "Get notified" and aria-label="Dialog". Which name wins?
choices: "Dialog", because the last attribute written wins
"Dialog Get notified", joined in document order
"Get notified", because aria-labelledby comes first
Neither, because two sources conflict and both are dropped
items.explanation: aria-labelledby wins outright in the accessible-name lookup.

items.prompt: What is the first rule of ARIA?
choices: Add a role to every element you ship
Use a native element when one exists
Avoid keyboard handling in custom widgets
items.explanation: Native elements ship the role and behavior for free.

items.prompt: Which keys activate a native button?
choices: Enter and Space
Space and Escape
Enter and Tab
items.explanation: Users expect both.

items.prompt: What does tabindex="0" do on a div?
choices: Gives it an accessible name
Turns it into a native button
Makes it reachable with Tab
items.explanation: It adds the element to the Tab order, nothing more.

items.prompt: An ARIA role is best described as...
choices: A purely visual style hint
A contract about behavior
A hint about page speed
items.explanation: Assistive tech trusts the role to describe how the control behaves.

items.prompt: A div with role="button" but no key handler is...
choices: Broken for keyboard users
Fully accessible already
Faster than a real button
items.explanation: The role promises behavior that is not there.

items.prompt: Which widget has no native HTML equivalent and may need ARIA?
choices: A save button
A text input
A tab panel
items.explanation: Custom widgets like tabs, comboboxes, and trees are what ARIA is for.

items.prompt: Does adding role="button" add keyboard behavior?
choices: Yes, both Enter and Space automatically
No, it only changes what is claimed
Yes, but only the Space key works
items.explanation: ARIA changes the tree, not the element's behavior.

items.prompt: Which is better: no ARIA or bad ARIA?
choices: No ARIA
Bad ARIA
They are identical
items.explanation: Bad ARIA makes false claims to assistive tech.

items.prompt: A custom dropdown has role="listbox" and role="option" but no keyboard handling. Compared with no roles at all, it is...
choices: Less trustworthy, since it promises behavior it lacks
More trustworthy, since the roles at least name the parts
Equal, since roles are only decorative labels
More trustworthy, since the mouse still works fine
items.explanation: The announcement sets expectations that the missing keys then break.
items.reference:
Native vs retrofitted
🟢 <button>: role, Tab focus, Enter + Space, name from text
🟠 <div role="button">: only the role, rest is hand-built
🔴 role without behavior = a false promise
⚖️ no ARIA beats bad ARIA
Why: a role is a contract about behavior, and only native elements keep the contract by default.
items.learnMore:
Why native wins

ARIA changes what the tree claims, not what the element does. Every row of behavior a native control gives free must be rebuilt by hand on a div, and each missed row breaks it silently.

Common mistake

Adding a role to look accessible without adding the keyboard behavior it promises.
items.reflection: Think of a sign that promises something the place does not deliver, like an "Exit" sign on a locked door. What does that false promise cost a person in a hurry?

items.prompt: A div has role="button", tabindex="0", and an onclick handler only. A keyboard user focuses it. What happens?
choices: Both Enter and Space activate it just as a real button does
Neither key activates it until a key handler is added
Enter activates it but Space does nothing at all
Space activates it but Enter does nothing at all
items.explanation: onclick does not fire from key presses on a div; a keydown handler must cover both keys.

The unplug-the-mouse test

➡️ Reach: in the Tab order once

items.prompt: Implement `linearize(channel)` for a channel value 0-255. Divide by 255 to get `c`; if `c <= 0.03928` return `c / 12.92`, otherwise return `Math.pow((c + 0.055) / 1.055, 2.4)`.

tests.description: small values use the linear branch

items.explanation: Stored color values are not proportional to light. The conversion has a small linear segment near black and a power curve above it; luminance must be computed from linear light.

items.prompt: Implement `passesAA(ratio)` returning true when normal-size body text with this contrast ratio meets AA.
items.explanation: AA needs at least 4.5:1 for body text. The boundary is inclusive, so exactly 4.5 passes.

items.prompt: Implement `passesAAA(ratio)` returning true when normal-size body text with this contrast ratio meets AAA.
items.explanation: AAA raises the body-text bar to 7:1. A ratio that is fine for AA, like 4.54, can still fail AAA.

items.prompt: Implement `passesAAText(ratio, isLarge)`. At AA, large text needs at least 3:1 and all other text needs at least 4.5:1.
items.explanation: Large text is easier to read at the same contrast, so AA relaxes its threshold to 3:1; pick the threshold first, then compare.

items.prompt: Implement `ratioFromLuminance(a, b)` for two relative luminances (0 to 1) in either order. Return `(lighter + 0.05) / (darker + 0.05)` rounded to 2 decimals using `Math.round(x * 100) / 100`.
items.explanation: The ratio always puts the lighter luminance on top, so the order of the arguments must not matter. The 0.05 terms stand for ambient light and keep black from dividing by zero.

items.prompt: Implement `wcagBand(ratio)` for normal text: return `"AAA"` at 7 or more, `"AA"` at 4.5 or more, otherwise `"fail"`.
items.explanation: Check the strictest threshold first. Checking AA first would label a 7:1 ratio as only AA.

items.prompt: Implement `grayOnWhite(gray)` returning the WCAG contrast ratio of a gray text (red = green = blue = `gray`, 0-255) on a white background, rounded to 2 decimals with `Math.round(x * 100) / 100`. Linearize the channel (divide by 255; `c <= 0.03928` uses `c / 12.92`, otherwise `Math.pow((c + 0.055) / 1.055, 2.4)`), and for gray the luminance equals the linear value. White has luminance 1.
items.explanation: For gray, all three channels are equal and the weights sum to 1, so luminance is just the linearized value. Dividing 1.05 by (luminance + 0.05) is the ratio against white, rounded at the end only.
items.reference:
Contrast = luminance ratio
🎚️ channel → linear light (0 to 1)
⚖️ weight: 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B
➗ ratio = (lighter + 0.05) / (darker + 0.05)
📏 AA 4.5:1 body, 3:1 large; AAA 7:1
Why: the formula is deterministic, so a pass or fail is a number, not an opinion.
items.learnMore:
Why not just look

Gray 118 on white is 4.54:1 and gray 120 is 4.42:1: near-identical to the eye but on opposite sides of AA. Only the computation decides.

Common mistake

Trusting that a color looks readable on a bright, high-quality monitor.
items.reflection: Think of another rule with a hard numeric edge, like a speed limit or an age cutoff. What goes wrong when people judge it by eye?
